en: Chapter Four: The Exhaustion and Extinction of Karmic Obstructions; Chapter Four: Repentance as Seen in Dreams (Part Three).
Regarding the Chapter on Repentance as Seen in Dreams, there is a threefold analysis: first, the purpose; second, the etymology; third, [the detailed exposition].
Explanation of the Objections.
There are four intentions for [this] coming:
first, the preceding two chapters clarify the fruits attained;...
Next, the following five chapters clarify the practices to be cultivated, which are divided into four sections:

the first two chapters clarify the preliminary practices for the stages (*bhūmi*); the next chapter clarifies the practices of the ten stages; the subsequent chapter serves as an explanation to resolve doubts and inspire aspirational practice; and the final chapter clarifies the practice of protecting the Dharma.
By means of dhāraṇīs, one protects the practice of the Dharma so that it does not regress.
Within the preliminary practices for the stages (*bhūmi*), the first is the practice of skillful means and the last is the practice of actual engagement.
If one wishes to attain the supreme fruit, one must first practice cultivation.
There are two aspects to this cultivation:
first, the abandonment of evil; second, the cultivation of goodness.
If evil is not eliminated, it is difficult to cultivate sublime conduct.
Thus, the *Ṣaṇmukhadhāraṇīsūtra* states: "If all the karmic deeds of Māra that I have committed have not first been repented, I shall never resolve my mind upon unsurpassed enlightenment."
Therefore, any existing transgressions must first be repented and extinguished.

Furthermore, as with the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the first two involve abandoning evil and the latter two involve cultivating goodness; thus, when about to practice sublime conduct, one is first instructed to perform repentance.
However, the mind of repentance is difficult to arouse instantaneously; therefore, the dream of the golden drum preaching the Dharma was used to awaken them.
Thus, the following text states: "This meritorious karma arises from your past offerings to the Buddhas, as well as through the majestic power and protection of all the Buddhas."
This chapter is composed because one wishes to eliminate the preliminary faults of karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*).

Although this chapter and the "Chapter on Eliminating Obstructions" (*Nivaraṇaviśodhana*) also include the cultivation of wholesome qualities—such as making aspirational prayers—they are designated as "abandoning unwholesome conduct" (*akuśalacaryā-vivarjana*) because they primarily clarify that specific subject matter.

Furthermore, each [chapter] is titled from its beginning as "Repentance" (Chān-hui) or "Chapter on the Elimination of Karmic Obstructions" (Mie-ye-zhang-pin), yet this does not mean that the cultivation of goodness is absent.
Second, the supreme practices cultivated do not exceed the Three Trainings (triśikṣā), namely: ethical discipline (śīla), meditative concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā).

Through ethical discipline (*śīla*), one is able to create the cause for departing from the evil realms; through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is able to create the cause for transcending the desire realm; and through wisdom (*prajñā*), one is able to create the cause for departing from the three realms.

Furthermore, ethical discipline serves as the foundation for meditative concentration, and meditative concentration serves as the foundation for wisdom, because it is only by taking ethical discipline as the basis that one attains concentration and wisdom.

The *Śālistamba Sūtra* (Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) states: "One should know that this precept is the dwelling place of all wholesome merits and virtues; it can give rise to various concentrations, meditations, and the wisdom that extinguishes suffering."

This confession is subsumed under the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*), which is the beginning of spiritual cultivation; therefore, this chapter is presented first to clarify its existence.

Third, the Buddha has three bodies—namely, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*)—which correspond respectively to the virtues of abandonment (*prahāṇa*), wisdom (*jñāna*), and power (*bala*).

That is to say, morality serves as the cause for the quality of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) by means of extinguishing evil; meditative concentration (*samādhi*) serves as the cause for the quality of benefit (*anuśaṃsā-guṇa*) by means of being able to produce emanations (*nirmāṇa*); and wisdom (*prajñā*) serves as the cause for the quality of knowledge (*jñāna-guṇa*) by means of being able to exercise decisive discernment.
Since the Dharma-body has the quality of abandonment as its fundamental basis, the causes for it are clarified first; thus, this chapter arises.

The fourth is for the sake of the appropriate occasion: first, because the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner, through the power of his past roots of goodness, came before the Buddha to manifest [his realization]; second, because it was appropriate for the assembly to first hear the method of repentance regarding dreams before they could attain awakening; therefore, this chapter has come forth.
According to the commentary by Paramārtha, there are eight causes and conditions.
Second, regarding the explanation of the name: in Sanskrit it is called *svapnadarśanāpatti-deśanā*.
*Svapna* here means "dream," *darśana* means "seeing," *āpatti* means "offense," and *deśanā* means "confession."
When a person has committed an offense, they must confess it to another; thus the transgression is eliminated, which is why it is called "declaring one's sins" (shuōzuì).
As for the term "repentance" (chànhuǐ), this follows the translations of ancient scholars and is not the precise explanation.
If one speaks of "confession" (chàn-huǐ), the Sanskrit term is *kṣamā*, which in meaning corresponds here to "forgiveness" or "apology.
Alternatively, it is called *kṣamā*, which is abbreviated here as "knowing weariness and detachment," and its meaning is also "reformation through repentance."
The term "confession" (*chànhuì*) is a corruption and abbreviation; it should properly be called the "Chapter on Confessing Sins as Seen in a Dream.

"Dream" refers to the seeing, and "sin" refers to the speaking; "dream" is the general category while "seeing" is the specific instance. By attaching the specific to the general, one says "the seeing within a dream," hence the title "Chapter on Confessing Sins as Seen in a Dream."
To resolve this difficulty, one asks:

Since Miaodang had not yet finished hearing the teaching when he returned home midway, why did he only go back to the Buddha to present his plea after hearing the teaching through a dream and performing repentance?
Answer: Gudu originally saw this because he had seen it in a dream; favorable conditions compelled him to return home.
If his body had not been asleep while among the assembly, how could such a dream have arisen?
Question:

Since the body of Wondrous Canopy was present in the assembly, why did [the Buddha] not directly show the method for repentance, but instead wait until he returned to his chamber and appeared in a dream to manifest the Golden Drum teaching on confession?
Answer:
At that time, it was appropriate for the assembly to hear the account of the dream before the confession could properly begin.
Furthermore, because of the past karmic conditions of Wondrous Banner (Miaochuang), he heard it and repented with a sincere heart.
He asked:

Question: Since the sound of confession manifested from the drum appeared through the convergence of past affinities and the Buddha’s majestic power, why did the Drum Manifest appear only within the assembly, while the Wondrous Banner saw it alone in a dream at night?
Answer: The capacities of those in the assembly differ; it was appropriate that they hear it through successive transmission.
Having further explained this for the sake of the aspiration of Wondrous Banner (Miaochuang), the others were led to understand it.
Question: When Wondrous Banner heard the teaching on repentance within his dream, did he thereby immediately accomplish the repentance of his own transgressions?
Answer: This is due to a past vow; one is only able to perform repentance upon being startled awake from a dream, for hearing the teaching while dreaming does not constitute repentance itself.

Therefore, the subsequent "Chapter on the Lotus Metaphor Praise" states: "May I, in future lives throughout immeasurable and boundless kalpas, constantly see the great golden drum within my dreams and hear it proclaiming the sounds of repentance."
It continues, saying: "In dreams at night, I constantly hear the sound of golden drums; by day, I perform repentance accordingly.

Since it states that one wishes to hear the sounds of repentance and then performs repentance during the day, this clarifies that one first hears [the sound] rather than performing the actual repentance immediately.

If that were not so, why would it be necessary to further explain the "Chapter on the Elimination of Karmic Obstructions" (Karmāvaraṇaviśuddhi-parivarta) for those whose dreams have already accomplished the act of repentance?
If you say it is intended to cause others to resolve to repent, how could the sins of one who has repented in a dream be simultaneously eliminated?
Within this chapter, the main text is divided into four sections:

first, the dream of Subhūti the Elder hearing the confession and the benefits obtained; second, his visit to the Buddha to recount it and awaken others; third, the World-Honored One’s praise, seal of approval, and revelation of its significance; fourth, the great assembly hearing the discourse and all vowing to practice it.

Sūtra: At that time, after the Bodhisattva Subhaketur had personally heard the sublime Dharma before the Buddha, he rejoiced with leaping joy, contemplated it with single-minded focus, and returned to his own abode.
The commentary states:
First, the section on the benefits gained through repentance as heard by Miaodang in a dream.
This is divided into two parts:
Upon first hearing the Dharma, his heart rejoiced and he departed after reflecting upon it; that same night, he dreamed of a golden drum proclaiming the sounds of repentance.
The former event was recorded by the author of the sutra, while the latter was a dream experienced by the recipient.
This is the first [point].

Hearing that his lifespan is immeasurable, our doubts were severed and our hearts rejoiced; we single-mindedly contemplated how the Great Compassionate World-Honored One employs skillful means, and we likewise resolved to aspire to practice for the benefit of both ourselves and others.
Sūtra: During the night, in a dream, he saw a great golden drum, its radiance dazzling like the solar disc.
The commentary states:
"The Dream Drum explains the confession."
Among these, there are four parts:
first, seeing a golden drum in a dream; second, beholding the Triple Gem because of that; third, hearing the drum preach the Dharma; and fourth, recollecting and upholding it after having heard it.
This is the first.

In this light, one beholds immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, seated upon lapis lazuli thrones beneath jeweled trees, surrounded by assemblies of immeasurable hundreds of thousands as they preach the Dharma.
The commentary states:

Because of beholding the Three Jewels, the sutra records that a certain brahmin struck a golden drum with a mallet, producing a great sound; within that sound, he recited subtle and wondrous verses (gāthās) explaining the dharma of repentance.
The commentary says: Regarding "hearing the drum and preaching the Dharma," the Sūtra states:
Having heard it, Miaochuang (Wonderful Banner) retained it all in memory and remained with his mindfulness fixed upon it.
The commentary says:
Having heard [this], he reflected upon and retained it.

When the night had passed until dawn, surrounded by an immeasurable assembly of hundreds of thousands and carrying various offerings, he departed from the city of Rājagṛha and proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain.
The commentary says:
"Approaching the Buddha to present his account.
First he approaches the Buddha, and afterwards he presents his account.

This refers to approaching the Buddha: first, the approach; second, the retinue; third, carrying the offerings; fourth, reaching the location; fifth, beholding the Buddha; sixth, observing his deportment; seventh, making offerings; eighth, circumambulating to the right; and ninth, withdrawing and standing aside.
These first four [disciples],
having approached the World-Honored One and prostrated at his feet, arranged incense and flowers, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
They praised him, saying:
The final five sections. Scripture:
With palms joined in reverence, he gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance.
The eulogy says:
This is the formal exposition.
First is the preliminary request for exposition, followed by the actual exposition.
Within the first part, there are further two sections:
This is the first of the two parts: the ritual for the initial invitation and the subsequent request for the teaching.
From the Sūtra: He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In a dream, I saw a brahmin holding a drumstick in his hand and striking a magnificent golden drum, producing a great sound. Within that sound, he recited subtle and wondrous verses explaining the dharma of repentance; I have memorized them all.”
The commentary states:
"The request to speak has two parts:
first, the presentation of what was seen and heard in the dream; second, the request for permission to proclaim it."
This is the first [section].
The Sūtra says: “I only pray that the World-Honored One will bestow great compassion and grant me leave to speak.
The Commentary says:
"Please grant us permission to proclaim it.
Then, in the presence of the Buddha, he spoke these verses:

"Last night, in my dream, I beheld a great golden drum; its form was exceedingly beautiful and sublime. It was encircled by golden light, like the orb of the blazing sun, its radiance shining everywhere, filling the realms of the ten directions."
They all behold the Buddhas beneath jeweled trees, each seated upon a lapis lazuli throne, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of countless beings who pay them reverent homage.
The commentary states: This is the formal exposition.
First is the introduction by the sūtra-reciter; second is the actual presentation of the teaching.
In total there are one hundred and fifty-six lines; among them, the first four lines consist of five characters per phrase, with four phrases forming one verse, thus resulting in four verses.
Next, there are twenty-two lines, each consisting of seven syllables, totaling eleven stanzas.
Next, there are thirty-eight stanzas, each consisting of five syllables.
Next, there are ninety-two lines, each composed of seven syllables, totaling forty-six stanzas.
If one follows the Western method of composing verses, all verses consist of four lines.
Regarding the types of lines, there are five:
first, the intermediate line; second, the initial line; third, the final line; fourth, the short line; and fifth, the long line.
If eight syllables are formed, it is called *pada* in Sanskrit; this is termed a "middle-length phrase," being neither too long nor too short.
When four such phrases form a single verse, it is called a *śloka*, consisting of thirty-two syllables.
If it is formed with six syllables or more, it is called the first phrase;
if it is formed with twenty syllables or more, it is called the latter phrase;
if it is formed with fewer than six syllables, it is called a short phrase.
Verses consisting of more than twenty-six syllables are termed *gāthā* of long lines;
this may be understood by analogy.

Now, in this sutra, according to the examination of the Sanskrit manuscript, there are instances where seventeen syllables constitute a line, or fifteen syllables, even down to three syllables being called a single line.

Now, where the prose passages were long, they have been condensed into seven-syllable verses, and where the prose passages were short, they have been condensed into five-syllable verses; thus, there are ninety-nine verses in total.
These are divided into two parts:
the first four verses briefly indicate what was heard and seen, while the subsequent ninety-five verses extensively set forth what was heard.
The first part consists of three sections:
the first line indicates the time of the dream; the next two lines and three phrases indicate what was seen; and the final verse indicates what was heard.
Within the section on what was seen, six lines describe seeing the drum, three lines describe seeing the Buddha, and two lines describe beholding the Saṃgha.
In the six lines, one sees the drum: in the first half-line, one sees the form of the drum; in the next line, one sees the light of the drum.
Dreaming of a golden drum signifies that one will hear the sound of the Buddha’s teaching on repentance, for it is worthy of being cherished and honored.
That his form is seen as wondrous signifies that this Great Being possesses the Brahma-voice.
That light pervades everywhere signifies that the nature of the teaching which expresses [the truth] is able to manifest the pervasive nature of principle.
"Like the blazing orb of the sun" signifies that the function of the teaching which expresses [the truth] can dispel all the darkness of unwholesomeness.
"Its radiance shines everywhere" signifies that the voice of a single flavor provides relief equally to both enemies and kin.

Those who see the Buddha and the great assembly are the Buddha and Sangha Jewels; hearing the drum that proclaims the Dharma is the Dharma Jewel. This signifies that by hearing the teaching, one attains the vision of the Three Jewels, and shall likewise achieve self-perfection.
Sūtra: “There was a brahmin who struck a golden drum with a staff; within the sound of that drum, he spoke these sublime verses.
Commentary: This indicates the hearing of the Dharma.
There are two parts:
the first half [of the verse] shows the person who can beat the drum; the subsequent half-verse describes hearing the drum preaching the Dharma.
There was a certain brāhmaṇa, representing one whose faculties were capable of being moved by the teaching.
Striking with a staff signifies that those who hear the teaching use the staff of their roots of goodness to strike the drum of the World-Honored One’s expressive teachings.
Alternatively, it represents a brahmin who is about to see the Buddha.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "That which is called the nature of a śramaṇa is also named 'brāhmaṇa' and is also called the 'Brahma-wheel,' because it is turned by the true Brahmā."
It should be understood that the World-Honored One is also called a true *brāhmaṇa* because he practices true purity.

Striking the drum of subsequently attained wisdom with the staff of great compassion, he causes the sound of the teaching to flow; since verses (*gāthā*) and other forms are provisionally established upon that sound, [he is so named].
This is the chanting of a gāthā verse from the Sūtra:
“The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* drum produces wondrous sounds that reach throughout the trichiliocosm.
The commentary states:
Below follows a detailed presentation of what has been heard, consisting of ninety-five verses, which are broadly divided into two parts:
first, eleven verses that generally indicate the benefits; second, eighty-four verses that specifically clarify the benefits.
The initial general heading is further divided into three parts:
first, half a verse designates the drum’s excellent sound; second, seven and a half verses designate the specific benefits; and third, three verses designate the superior causes for the latter.
This is the first [verse].
The Sūtra says: "It can extinguish the most grievous sins of the three miserable realms, as well as all the sufferings and calamities among human beings.
By the majestic power of the sound of this golden drum, all obstacles of affliction are forever extinguished; fear is severed and one is brought to peace and security, just like the Sovereign Muni."
The commentary states:
Within the initial section that sets forth the specific benefits, there follow three successive expositions on confession, aspiration, and so forth.

However, the first two successive expositions provide a mutual clarification through elliptical abbreviation, while the third successive exposition treats both confession and the others in full detail.

In this present outline, the first four and a half verses collectively outline the first two sections, which briefly clarify the benefits of confession and so forth; the subsequent three verses outline the third section below, which extensively clarifies the benefits of confession and so forth.
The first section is divided into two parts:
first, two and a half verses indicating freedom from suffering; second, two verses indicating the attainment of happiness.
Within the first part on freedom from suffering, one and a half verses indicate freedom from suffering and one verse praises the Buddha.

Within this section on the departure from suffering, the first half-verse describes the departure from the fruits of suffering, while the subsequent verse describes the departure from the causes of suffering.
Evil karma of superior or middling degree invites retribution in the three miserable realms; these are termed "extremely grave offenses."
Inferior-grade evil karma brings about suffering among humans, namely the pain of separation from loved ones, old age, sickness, death, and so forth.
Within the section on the causes for escaping suffering, three phrases present the causes for liberation, while one phrase provides an illustration.
The analogy has two meanings:
first, it illustrates sentient beings attaining the cause for the cessation of suffering, like the Honored Muni;
second, it illustrates that the golden drum is also like the Muni, being able to proclaim the noble Dharma that extinguishes the suffering of sentient beings.

Sūtra: “Within the great ocean of birth and death, the Buddha accumulated practices and cultivated all-encompassing wisdom; he is able to cause sentient beings to be fully endowed with the factors of enlightenment, so that they ultimately all return to the ocean of merit.”
The commentary states:
There are two parts to this praise of the Buddha;
the first half-verse praises the virtue of self-benefit, and the second half-verse praises the virtue of benefiting others.
One who possesses the factors of enlightenment is able to cause sentient beings to cultivate great bodhi;
when all the merits of the associated retinue are fully perfected, that is itself great bodhi.
Ultimately, all return to the ocean of merit, which is the Great Nirvāṇa.

Alternatively, the possession of the factors of enlightenment enables the fulfillment of the causes of cultivation, while returning to the ocean of merit enables the fulfillment of the attainment of the fruit.

Sūtra: “From this golden drum emerges a wondrous sound, universally causing all who hear it to obtain the Brahma-voice, realize the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi, and constantly turn the pure, sublime Wheel of Dharma.”
The commentary states:
This clarifies the attainment of bliss.
The first verse attains the bliss of self-benefit; the latter verse attains the bliss of benefiting others.
This attainment of one's own benefit and happiness has three aspects:
first, causing the acquisition of the Brahma-voice; second, realizing Bodhi; and third, attaining Nirvana.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 95, the turning of the Wheel of Dharma includes both self-turning and turning for others. Within self-turning, there are five characteristics:

First is the attainment of the object to be attained; second is the means for its attainment; third is the attainment of that which is to be attained; fourth is to cause others to develop deep faith and understanding regarding what one has personally realized by means of their own mental continuums; and fifth is to cause others to develop deep faith and understanding regarding what they themselves have realized.

This constant turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma constitutes the third [characteristic], for it serves to attain the fruit of great *nirvāṇa*; this is because it is preceded by *bodhi* and followed by the preaching of the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings.
This turning of the wheel of Dharma is itself nirvāṇa.
The meaning of the wheel of Dharma is as clarified in the *Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra*. The sūtra states:

“Abiding for inconceivable kalpas, he preaches the Dharma according to capacities to benefit all sentient beings; he is able to sever the flowing stream of afflictions and manifold sufferings, so that greed, hatred, delusion, and the like are all extinguished.”
The commentary states:
One attains the happiness of others by three means:
first, remaining in this world for the sake of sentient beings; second, preaching the Dharma; and third, severing afflictions.
The "stream of manifold sufferings" refers to the three—afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering.

By severing the bondage of the object (*ālambana-bandhana*), once the bondage of the object is exhausted, the grasping (*rāga*) and other factors that constitute the subject also perish accordingly; this is the severance of the bondage of the subject (*ālambaka-bandhana*).
Having become free from all bonds, they attain peace and happiness.

The Sūtra says: "If there are sentient beings dwelling in the evil realms, their bodies completely enveloped by the fierce flames of a great fire, should they hear the sound of this wondrous drum, they will immediately be able to leave suffering behind and take refuge in the Buddha."
The commentary states:
The final three verses of the hymn indicate the subsequent extensive confession and so forth, which are twofold:

the first verse indicates that by hearing the Dharma while possessing faults, one may resolve and repent to leave suffering behind; the latter two verses show that by hearing the sound of the drum, one attains peace and happiness.
This is the first [point].
Question:

This is a dream of the Exquisite Banner (Sudhvaja) himself regarding a golden drum; since others do not hear it, how can it be said that "in a place where great fires pervade the bodies of those in the evil destinies, they hear the sound of the exquisite drum and leave suffering to take refuge in the Buddha"?
Answer: These aforementioned accounts of others receiving benefits and so forth were all seen in a dream by the Bodhisattva Subhaketu; in reality, no one else heard the sound of the drum.
This meaning indicates that if any class of sentient beings were to hear the Buddha’s teaching, they would obtain such benefits.

Sūtra: “They all attained the accomplishment of the knowledge of past lives, being able to remember hundreds of thousands of past births; with perfect mindfulness, they all called to mind the Honored One, the Muni, and were able to hear the profound teaching of the Tathāgata.”

By hearing the sublime and wondrous sound of the golden drum, one shall always be able to draw near to all Buddhas; one will be able to completely abandon all evil karma and purely cultivate all categories of pure goodness.
Commentary: This indicates the attainment of bliss.
It is divided into six parts:

The first half-verse attains the knowledge of past lives; the next line attains right mindfulness; the next line [attains] hearing the Dharma; the next two lines [attain] proximity to the Buddha; the next line [attains] separation from evil; and the final line [attains] the cultivation of goodness.

Sūtra: "All sentient beings, whether devas or humans, who pray with profound reverence and utmost sincerity, shall hear the wondrous sound of the golden drum, which is able to fulfill all their aspirations."
The commentary states:
The following three verses indicate that there are other superior causes for the remaining types [of bodhisattvas].
There are three [points]:

The first verse indicates the fulfillment of the vow according to one's heart; the second verse indicates the attainment of freedom from suffering; the third verse indicates the attainment of peace and happiness.
This is the first [verse].

Sūtra: "Sentient beings fallen into the Avīci Hell, their bodies scorched by the fierce blaze of raging fires, have no protector as they wander in saṃsāra—those who hear this shall be able to extinguish their suffering."
The commentary states:
"Attaining" indicates the departure from suffering.
This is stated according to the most significant case, namely, the departure from the suffering of the *ānantarya* (immediate) hells.

Alternatively, the first half-verse may refer to liberation from the suffering of the immediate hells, while the second half-verse refers generally to liberation from the sufferings of all realms and destinies.

As the Sūtra says: "Among humans, devas, hungry ghosts, and animals, whatever various sufferings and hardships are currently being experienced—all shall, upon hearing the wondrous resonance emitted by the golden drum, be granted liberation through the removal of suffering."
The commentary states:
This indicates the attainment of bliss.
The first half-verse restates the suffering from which one is liberated; the second half-verse distinguishes the bliss that is attained.
Sūtra: “The Two-legged Honored Ones who eternally abide throughout the worlds of the ten directions, we pray that with hearts of great compassion, you will take pity upon us and remember us.
Sentient beings have no refuge and no protector; for the sake of such as these, may you act as their great refuge.”
The commentary states:
The following eighty-four verses specifically clarify the benefits.
These are divided into four parts:

First, the twenty-five verses constitute the first section, which elucidates the confession and aspiration; next, from "I only pray that the Buddhas of the ten directions... onwards, the thirteen verses constitute the second section, which elucidates the confession and aspiration; next, the forty-three verses beginning with the seven-syllable meter constitute the third section, which elucidates the confession and aspiration; and finally, the four verses beginning with "If there are men or women... explain the superior exhortation to practice.

However, among the three successive cycles of confession and aspiration, the first cycle primarily involves the confession of afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the second cycle primarily involves the confession of karmic hindrances (*karmāvaraṇa*), and the third cycle primarily involves the confession of retributive hindrances (*vipākāvaraṇa*); therein lies the difference between their concise and extensive treatments.

Confession (*pratideśanā*) is properly termed "declaring one's offenses. Its essential nature consists of wholesome remorse and the verbal karma (*vākkarman*) it engenders; if one includes that which initiates it, it also possesses mental karma (*manaskarman*); and if prostrations are performed, it also possesses bodily karma (*kāyakarman*). Fully, its nature should be understood as wholesome remorse together with the three types of karma it engenders.
The first section, "Furthermore," consists of three parts:

the first two verses request protection and describe the correct taking of refuge; the next fourteen verses clarify the practice of repentance; and the final nine verses clarify the making of aspirational prayers.
The first part consists of four sections:

the first two lines identify the object of refuge; the next two lines request compassionate regard; the following two lines declare the lack of protection; and the final two lines request that [the Buddha] act as a refuge.

Among sentient beings, there are those with no feet, many feet, four feet, and two feet; among these, humans and devas—the two-footed—are superior to the others, and the Buddha is further the most honored among the two-footed.
To grieve at their suffering and to take pity on their lack of joy is the very embodiment of compassion (*karuṇā* and *maitrī*).
To vow not to abandon them is called mindfulness (*anusmṛti*).

To cast oneself [before them] is called taking refuge (*śaraṇa-gamana*); to rely upon them is called dependence (*niśraya*). To extract them from suffering is called rescue (*trāṇa*); to bestow happiness upon them is called protection (*rakṣā*).
Sūtra: "Whatever sins I have previously committed, those most heavy and evil karmas, I now, before the One of Ten Powers, confess with a sincere heart.
Commentary: The following fourteen verses clarify the confession of transgressions.
This is divided into three parts:
first, one verse that provides the heading; second, twelve verses that provide the analysis; and third, one verse that provides the conclusion.
This is the initial heading.
"Sin" (āpatti) is a term for censuring faults.
Even extremely grave evil karma is described as censuring faults; conversely, even a minor offense is termed an extremely grave committed sin and evil karma.
In the general discourse on repenting all three types of karma, it says "all" in the sutra:
"I did not believe in the Buddhas, nor did I revere my elders or kin; I did not strive to cultivate various virtues, but constantly committed all manner of evil deeds."
The commentary states:
The following provides a detailed analysis, divided into twelve parts.
The first verse clarifies the confession of evil karma created through lack of faith, shamelessness, and so forth.
"Disrespect" means not honoring the worthy and not applying oneself to the cultivation of goodness;
that is, not valuing virtue, which leads one to commit evil.
Sūtra: “Or, relying on one’s own nobility, lineage, and wealth and status, one indulges in heedlessness during the prime of youth and constantly commits various evil karmas.
Commentary: The second verse repents of the sinful karma created through arrogance and other such afflictions.

First, relying on the dignity of one's virtue; second, relying on the nobility of one's lineage; third, relying on abundant wealth; fourth, relying on official rank; fifth, relying on youth, longevity, and freedom from illness.
Exalting oneself and disparaging others, one gives rise to evil through pride and becomes intoxicated with arrogance.
Thus, by means of conceit, one commits evil; furthermore, practicing heedlessness, one fails to guard or cultivate [the mind], and thereby creates unwholesome karma.
Sūtra: “The mind constantly gives rise to perverse thoughts, the mouth utters evil words, one does not perceive one’s own transgressions, and one perpetually creates various evil karmas. Commentary:
The third verse repents the evil karma created by the two actions of mind and speech.
Sūtra: “Constantly performing the conduct of a fool, with the mind shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, following along with unwholesome friends, one constantly creates various evil karmas.
Commentary: The fourth verse repents the creation of evil karma through delusion (*moha*).
Sūtra: "Whether due to various forms of play and amusement, or again out of harbored grief and affliction, being entangled by greed and hatred, I have committed various evils.
Commentary: The fifth verse repents the evil karma created because of greed and hatred.
Amusement and pleasure are greed; grief and affliction are hatred.
Greed and hatred are the seeds; the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are the active manifestations (*samudācāra*), such as the eight envelopments and so forth, where two are cited to include the rest.
Sūtra: “Because I associated with unwholesome people, because of a mind of stinginess and envy, and because I practiced flattery and deception out of poverty, I have committed various evils.
Commentary: The sixth confession concerns associating with evil friends and the minor secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
To amass wealth without relinquishing it and to be base and stingy is called *mātsarya* (avarice).
To be unable to endure the prosperity of others out of envy and jealousy is called *īrṣyā* (envy).
To entangle others with a net by acting deviously to comply with their wishes is called *śāṭhya* (deceit).
To harbor ulterior motives while feigning the appearance of virtue is called "deception.
As the Sūtra says: "Although I do not delight in the multitude of transgressions, because of the presence of fear and because I have not attained self-mastery, I have committed various evils."
Commentary: The seventh confession concerns the commission of evil karma out of fear.
Although one’s mind may not delight in committing transgressions, one might nevertheless commit evil karma due to fear for one's life, wealth, or other such difficulties.
Or, dwelling in a lowly and base position, being driven and coerced by others without autonomy, one thus creates evil karma.
As the Sūtra says: "Whether due to a restless mind, or because of anger and resentment, or the affliction of hunger and thirst, I have committed various evils."
The commentary states:
The eighth confession concerns the commission of evil karma due to the great secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and so forth;
it concerns the commission of various evil karmas because one is oppressed and tormented by hunger, thirst, and desire.
Sūtra: "Because of food, drink, clothing, and lustful attachment to women, I was scorched by the fires of affliction; therefore, I committed various evils.
Commentary: The ninth confession concerns the commission of various evil karmas due to greed.
Sūtra: “Regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, I failed to give rise to a mind of reverence; for all such transgressions, I now repent them all.
Regarding the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas as well, I lacked a mind of reverence; for all such transgressions, I now repent them all.”
Commentary: The tenth confession concerns the commission of various evils due to a lack of reverence for the Triple Gem.
The Sūtra says: "For slandering the True Dharma out of ignorance, for being unfilial toward my parents, and for committing such manifold transgressions as these, I now confess them all."
The commentary states:
The eleventh repentance concerns the evil karma produced by the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).
Regarding the five heinous crimes as explained in the Mahayana sutras, they are not taught as being common to the three vehicles.

Regarding the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), according to the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra*: first, one must not destroy stūpas or monasteries, burn scriptures or images, or steal the property of the Triple Gem;
second, one must not slander the teachings of the Three Vehicles by claiming they are not the holy doctrine, nor create obstacles, hindrances, concealments, or coverings for them;

third, regarding any ordained person—whether possessing the precepts or not, whether upholding or violating them—one must not strike, scold, revile, or find fault with them, nor subject them to confinement, force their return to lay life, compel their labor, or take their lives.
Fourth, one must not kill one’s father, harm one’s mother, shed the blood of a Buddha, cause a schism in the Saṃgha, or kill an Arhat;
fifth, one must not slander [the Dharma] by denying cause and effect, nor constantly practice the ten unwholesome karmas throughout the long night.
Now, this slandering of the Dharma is the second *ānantarya* offense, and being unfilial toward one's parents is the fourth *ānantarya* offense.
As the Sūtra says: "Due to the power of ignorance and pride, as well as greed and hatred, I have committed such manifold sins; I now repent of them all."
The commentary states:
The twelfth confession concerns the commission of evil karma due to the three unwholesome roots.
As for the mention of "arrogance," it is included because it arises from the unwholesome root of delusion.
Furthermore, according to the first section, this single verse concludes the confession of all previously committed transgressions.

The Sūtra says: "In the worlds of the ten directions, I have made offerings to countless Buddhas; may I thereby vow to deliver sentient beings and cause them to leave behind all suffering and hardship."
"May all sentient beings be established in the ten stages; having perfected merit and wisdom, may they attain Buddhahood to guide the deluded masses.
Commentary: The following nine verses express these aspirations.
May it be that subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhājñāna*), desire (*chanda*), or resolve (*adhimokṣa*) constitutes the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).
Since one has already paid homage and made a formal declaration, this also includes the three types of action (*trikarma*) thereby initiated as its substance.

Subsequently, subsequent knowledge, desire, and resolve constitute the essential nature; those arising from the aspiration of body and speech, as well as the mental action associated with and arising from that aspiration, are all termed "aspiration."
If it were not so, what would be subsumed?
Within this, there are four parts:
the first two verses concern benefiting sentient beings; one verse concerns the aspiration that they may be freed from suffering; and one verse concerns the aspiration that they may attain happiness.

Sūtra: “For the sake of all sentient beings, I have practiced asceticism for hundreds of thousands of kalpas; by the power of great wisdom, I shall cause them all to emerge from the ocean of suffering.
For the sake of all conscious beings, I expound this most profound sūtra, the supreme *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, which can eliminate all evil karma.”
The commentary states:
The following two verses concern the aspiration for the arousal of practice.
One verse aspires to cultivate merit and wisdom for the sake of sentient beings; one verse aspires to preach the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

Sūtra: “If a person, throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, has committed various most grievous sins, by being able to confess them for even a brief moment, all evils will be completely eliminated.
By relying on this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, performing such repentance, one is thereby able to swiftly exhaust all karmas of suffering.”
"May they cultivate hundreds of thousands of kinds of supreme concentrations, inconceivable dhāraṇīs, the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, always without weariness.
The commentary states:
The following three verses express the aspiration for others to practice.
The first two verses express the aspiration to exhort others to eliminate evil, while the final verse expresses the aspiration to exhort others to cultivate goodness.
The Sūtra states: "May I reach the tenth stage, the place replete with precious jewels; may I fulfill the merits of a Buddha and deliver beings from the stream of birth and death."
"Regarding the oceans of all Buddhas, the treasuries of their most profound merit, and their wondrous wisdom that is difficult to conceive—I shall cause them all to attain full perfection.
Commentary: The following two verses express the vow for the fulfillment of one's own fruition.

The first verse expresses the aspiration that the causes may be fulfilled to benefit sentient beings; the latter verse expresses the aspiration that the fruits may be perfected to be spontaneously possessed by oneself.
Although the term "to cause" (*liṅ*) applies generally to both self and others, the intended meaning here is taken as causing oneself to possess [the qualities].
Previously, I vowed to be born [in the Pure Land] so that I might abide in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), perfect my merit and wisdom, attain Buddhahood, and finally lead all deluded beings across.
As the Sūtra says: “May the Buddhas of the ten directions observe and protect me; may they all, with hearts of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), graciously accept my repentance.”
The commentary states:
Below are thirteen verses; this second section primarily concerns the repentance of karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*).
The text is divided into four parts:
The first ten verses clarify confession; the next verse clarifies sympathetic joy; the next verse clarifies the generation of the aspiration; and the final verse clarifies dedication.
Within the section on confession, there are three parts:
this first verse requests protection and describes the basis.
Sūtra: "Whatever evil karma I have created throughout many kalpas, which gives rise to suffering and affliction—out of compassion, I pray that it be eliminated.
Commentary: The following eight verses clearly explain the confession of transgressions.
This is further divided into four parts;
the first verse here provides a general summary of the confession and vow.
The Sūtra says: "I have committed various evil deeds, And my mind is constantly filled with anxiety and fear; Throughout the four modes of deportment, I have never experienced a thought of joy."
The Commentary states:
The following verse describes the depth of his own sorrow.
The Sūtra says: "The Buddhas possess great compassion and are able to remove the fears of sentient beings; I pray that you accept my confession and cause me to be free from sorrow and suffering."
The commentary states:
This is a prayer for permission to repent.
The Sūtra says: "I have afflictive obscurations as well as various karmic retributions; I pray that you will wash them clean with the water of great compassion."
The commentary states:
Next, the following five verses constitute the vow of repentance for the purpose of eliminating [obstacles].
This is further divided into four parts:
This first verse is a vow to repent and extinguish the three obstructions.
Because the Buddha, through his great compassion, extinguishes the fires of the three obstructions and further removes the defilement of transgressions, he is likened to water.
The Sūtra says: "Whatever sins I have committed in the past, as well as the evil karma I am currently creating—I confess them all with a sincere heart and pray that they may all be cleansed away."
"Regarding all evil karmas of the future, I shall guard against them so they do not arise; even if I should happen to transgress, I will never dare to conceal it.
The commentary states:
The following two verses express the vow to repent for the sins of the three periods of time.
*Jian* (蠲) also means to eliminate.
Regarding what has already been committed in the past and present, one repents with the vow to eliminate it;
regarding what has not yet been committed in the future, one vows to repent and guard against it so that it does not arise.
Sūtra: “The three actions of body, the four kinds of speech, and the three types of mental karma bind all sentient beings, continuing in succession from time immemorial.
Through these three modes of conduct, one commits the ten non-virtuous deeds; all such manifold transgressions, I now confess.”
The commentary states:
The following two verses express the vow to repent for the offenses of the three karmas.
This is identical to the confession explained in the fourth chapter of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, which says: "Three times three makes nine kinds; they arise from the three afflictions."

Regarding the combination of nine types: this refers to the aforementioned three types of karma, the three time periods, and the three types of retributive karma—namely, karma to be experienced in the next life, in the present life, and in subsequent lives—which together constitute nine.

Now, by adding the three obstacles and excluding the karma of the three retributions, this sutra takes a general perspective while that treatise focuses on the specific experience; because there is a distinction between them, both result in nine [categories], each without contradiction.
These nine all arise from greed, hatred, and delusion; thus, it is said they arise from the three afflictions.
Furthermore, that treatise asks:
among the three types of feeling-conducive [actions], there are those that are determinate and those that are indeterminate; how are these eliminated through repentance?
That treatise answers:
"Nor is it the case that all [karma] is extinguished.
If it were fixed retribution, one would wish to repay it in this very life."
This is also stated based on the certainty of retribution while the timing is uncertain;
if both the time and the retribution were certain, it would not be discussed at all.
This is said with reference to those capable of middling repentance, for if one can perform superior repentance, all offenses are eliminated.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If one enters my Dharma, there is no fixed [karmic result].
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Fixed retribution is established based on those who are not yet liberated."
This intention refers to those who have not yet planted the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); based on them, karma with fixed retribution (*niyata-vipāka*) is established.
If, however, one has planted the factors conducive to liberation, then [the nature of such karma] is generally indeterminate (*aniyata*).
That is not so; otherwise, how could sentient beings enter the state of a noble one (ārya) through cultivation in only three lifetimes?
It is not because all [beings] possess only the fixed retribution of three lifetimes.
The meaning of the ten paths of action (karmapatha) is as explained in a separate chapter.
Sūtra: "I have committed various evil karmas; their bitter retribution I must receive myself. Now, before all the Buddhas, I repent them all with utmost sincerity.
Commentary: The following one verse belongs to the conclusion of the personal confession.
Sūtra: “Whatever wholesome karmas exist here in Jambudvīpa and in other world-systems, I now rejoice in them all.
Commentary: This is the second rejoicing within the second section.
"Following" (*anugata*) means to accord with; "rejoicing" (*pramuditā*) refers to the state of being delighted.

Following thus takes the three factors of faith (*śraddhā*), aspiration (*chanda*), and resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) as its essence. Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "That which is characterized by sealing and acceding has resolute conviction as its essence."
If one delights in compliance, its essence is precisely desire.
Since patience is the cause of faith and desire is the fruit of faith, faith along with its cause and fruit constitutes its accompanying essence.

Joy (*muditā*) is the feeling of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*); alternatively, this joy does not necessarily refer to the feeling of joy, but rather is a conventional designation for the collective totality of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-samūha*) termed "rejoicing.
Alternatively, it is simply the absence of envy; thus, the immeasurable joy has non-envy as its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
This explanation is correct.
Because one rejoices in accordance with [another's] arising [of merit], it is called "rejoicing" (*anumodanā*); or, because one both follows and rejoices, it is termed "rejoicing.

As the Sūtra says: "May they leave behind the ten unwholesome paths of action, Cultivate the ten wholesome paths, Abide securely within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), And constantly behold the Buddhas of the ten directions."
The commentary states:
This is the third aspiration.
The Sūtra says: “By means of the merit and wisdom cultivated through my body, speech, and mind, may I, by virtue of these roots of goodness, swiftly attain unsurpassed wisdom.”
Commentary: Dedication has subsequent wisdom as its essence.
Another interpretation is that both verses are expressions of aspiration: the first concerns the cause and the latter the result.
"Now, in the presence of the One of Ten Powers, I openly confess my manifold sufferings and hardships."
The commentary states:
The following forty-two verses constitute the third section, which extensively explains the practice of repentance and aspiration, primarily focusing on the repentance for karmic obstacles.
The text is divided into five parts:

The first four verses express repentance; the next eleven verses praise the Buddha’s virtues; the following twenty-five verses set forth vows; the next single verse expresses sympathetic joy; and the final single verse dedicates the merit.
Within the initial section on repentance, the text is further divided into three parts; this first half-verse serves as a general heading for the submission of one’s sincerity.

Sūtra: “The difficulty of the delusions of the ignorant within the three realms of existence; the difficulty of constantly creating extremely grave evil karma; the difficulty of the accumulation of my own desires and perversities; the difficulty of the constant arising of craving and the resulting cycle of rebirth; the difficulty of being attached to this world; the difficulty of the afflictions of all foolish people; the difficulty of a mad mind that is distracted and inverted; the difficulty of associating with evil friends; the difficulty of being stained by greed within birth and death; the difficulty of committing sins through the darkness and dullness of hatred and ignorance; the difficulty of being born in the eight unfavorable states; and the difficulty of never having accumulated merit.”
The commentary states:
These three verses separately repent for various obstacles.
The three verses consist of twelve lines, with each line representing one obstacle.

1. The difficulty of ordinary beings not understanding the fruit of suffering; 2. The difficulty of constantly creating evil karma over a long period of time; 3. The difficulty of accumulating [karma] through the conception of "mine"; 4. The difficulty of transmigrating through the three realms due to craving; 5. The difficulty of being attached to worldly pleasant fruits; 6. The difficulty of giving rise to delusions based on an ordinary body; 7. The difficulty of giving rise to perversions through the distraction of a deviant mind; 8. The difficulty of being seized by evil friends; 9. The difficulty of being defiled by and attached to birth and death without understanding them; 10. The difficulty of committing sins due to the three poisons as causes; 11. The difficulty of being born with the retribution of unfavorable conditions (*akṣaṇa*); 12. The difficulty of not having planted roots of goodness since beginningless time.
This mind, due to evil karma, has been born into states of no leisure; due to the failure to cultivate goodness, transgressions have arisen.
Therefore, I now repent for them all. As the Sūtra says: "I now, before the Most Victorious Ones, repent of my boundless sinful karmas."
The commentary states:
The latter half of this verse concludes by expressing repentance for all transgressions.

The Sūtra says: "I now take refuge in all the Sugatas; I prostrate to the Unsurpassed Honored One, an ocean of virtues. Like a great mountain of gold illuminating the ten directions, I pray that you will compassionately and mercifully accept me."
The commentary states:
The following eleven verses praise the Buddha’s virtues.
The text is divided into three parts:

The first verse provides a general summary of the homage and praise; the next five verses offer praise according to the partial perception of his virtues; and the final five verses offer praise for the inexhaustibility of his virtues.
This is the first [verse].

Sūtra: “The color of his body is pure golden light, free from defilement; his eyes are like clear, deep-blue lapis lazuli. He is the Honored One of auspicious majesty and renown; with the sun of great compassion and wisdom, he dispels all darkness.”
Commentary: This is a praise according to one's capacity for seeing virtue.
Among the thirteen kinds of virtues praised herein, there are four:

The first line praises the virtue of the golden light of his body; the next line praises the virtue of the deep blue purity of his eyes; the next line praises the virtue of his majestic power and renown; and the final line praises the virtue of his compassion and wisdom that dispel darkness.

Sūtra: “The sun-like radiance of the Buddha is ever-pervasive; it is perfectly pure, stainless, and free from all dust. The moon-like illumination of the Muni is exceedingly cool, able to dispel the fever of afflictions in sentient beings.”
The commentary states:
This [verse] possesses two virtues. The first half-verse praises the virtue of omniscience free from defilement; the second half-verse praises the virtue of enabling the realization of nirvāṇa.
This is because the Muni, by means of the coolness of nirvāṇa, can remove the heat of the afflictions of sentient beings.

Sūtra: “Adorned throughout by the thirty-two marks, with all eighty secondary characteristics fully perfected; his merit is inconceivable and peerless, like the flowing light of the sun illuminating the world.”
The commentary states:

This [verse] possesses three virtues. The first line praises the virtue of the thirty-two major marks; the next line praises the virtue of the eighty minor marks; and the subsequent half-verse praises the virtue of accomplishing sentient beings.

As stated in the *Mahālaṃkāra-śāstra*: "For example, just as the midday sun [shines], so too is the generation of the mind (cittotpāda) associated with the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); just as the sun ripens grain, it brings sentient beings to maturity."
If the *Ekottarika Āgama* says: "When the sun rises, there are four things:
first, at the time of sunrise, all darkness is dispelled; second, farmers engage in their labors; third, the various birds all sing; fourth, infants cry."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"When the sun rises and all darkness is dispelled, it is a metaphor for the appearance of a Buddha in the world, who removes the darkness of ignorance and illuminates all classes of sentient beings with clarity."

Those who collectively cultivate the field are like donors and patrons who, according to the season, provide clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, mattresses and requisites, as well as medicine for the treatment of illness.
The singing of the hundred birds is like the various eminent Dharma masters who are able to expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
The crying of the infant is a metaphor for the evil Māra, whose mind is filled with great sorrow and distress upon seeing the Buddha appear in the world.

The Sūtra says: "His form is as pure and stainless as lapis lazuli; like the full moon dwelling in the void, his golden body is reflected by a wondrous net of crystal, adorned with manifold rays of light."
The commentary states:
This [verse] possesses two virtues.

The first half-verse praises the virtue of manifesting in accordance with responsive conditions, as described in the "Moon Simile" chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding the perception of the partial and the full, and so forth.
The subsequent half-verse praises the virtue of the *Jvālāmāla-vyūha* (Flame-Network Array).
It is of exquisite vaidūrya, white and red in color, as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "Like within pure vaidūrya, the image of true gold appears within," and so forth.

Sūtra: “Within the violent torrent of the suffering of birth and death, one is swept away by the waters of old age, sickness, and sorrow. Such an ocean of suffering is difficult to endure; may the Buddha-sun extend its radiance so that it may be forever exhausted.”
The commentary states:
This single verse praises the virtue of severing the cycle of birth and death for others.
As for the term "floods" (*ogha*), it refers to the four floods:
First, the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), which refers to the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm;
second, the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), which refers to the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the two higher realms;
third, the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*), which refers to the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in the three realms.
The fourth, the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*), refers to the ignorance of the three realms pertaining to both the paths of seeing and cultivation.
By this principle, the first three [floods] all exclude ignorance.
However, when various treatises describe the afflictions as floods, they do so based on their causal nature.
This explains that the suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is a "flood" (*ogha*), which refers to the fruit [of suffering].

Alternatively, cause and effect may be combined and termed "birth and death"; the drowning and drifting of sentient beings through old age, sickness, and sorrow is like a flood, and its profound depth and vastness make it difficult to cross, like a sea of suffering.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 70, states: "The five dharmas resemble the great ocean of birth and death, and thus receive the name 'great ocean.
This is because they resemble it in five ways: first, by the boundlessness of their location; second, by their profundity;"
Third, because they are similar in being difficult to traverse;
fourth, because they are similar in being inedible—this means that just as the great ocean is entirely bitter and inedible, so too is saṃsāra, wherein nothing is to be relished;

fifth, because they are similar in being the basis for great treasures—this means that just as all manner of jewels depend upon the ocean, so too within saṃsāra one attains the merits of the three vehicles.
Among these five meanings, we now take the first four to refer to what is "unbearable," which the sun-like light of the Buddha’s wisdom scorches until it is completely dried up.
The Sūtra says: "I now prostrate to the All-Knowing One, the rare and honored one of the trichiliocosm, whose radiant body is like purple-gold, adorned with all manner of exquisite marks."
The commentary states:
The following five verses constitute the praise for the inexhaustibility of his virtues.
This section is divided into two parts:
This first verse is a general salutation and praise.
As the scripture says: "As the volume of the great ocean is difficult to know, as the atoms of the great earth are incalculable, as Mount Sumeru is beyond measure, and as space has no limit."

The virtues of all Buddhas are likewise; no sentient beings can know them, even if they were to contemplate them with earnest reflection for immeasurable eons; there is none who can reach the shore of their ocean of merit.

All the mountains and peaks upon this great earth may be broken down into atoms and thus counted; the drops of the oceans may be measured with the tip of a hair; yet the merit of the Buddha can never be reckoned.
All sentient beings together praise the World-Honored One’s renown and all his virtues; his pure marks and signs are wondrously adorned, their measure and limits beyond calculation.
The commentary states:
The following four verses present specific praises of his virtues.
These four verses are divided into four parts:

The first verse praises his virtues by means of analogies; the next verse praises his transcendence of conceptual constructions; the next verse praises his transcendence of calculation; and the final verse praises his transcendence of verbal expression.
Daotong’s *Commentary on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* exceeds the four-part version [of Kumārajīva].
Furthermore, the first verse either praises, in respective order, the Buddha's four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, or it praises these virtues collectively.
There are four such types: first, virtues as profound as the ocean; second, virtues as numerous as motes of dust; third, virtues as lofty as mountains; and fourth, virtues as vast as space.
As stated in the fourth chapter of the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*: "Furthermore, there are ten qualities of a bodhisattva that are like the great ocean."

What are the ten? First, it is a great treasury of jewels; second, it is deep and vast, difficult to cross; third, it is expansive and boundless; fourth, it becomes progressively deeper; fifth, it does not dwell together with afflictions; sixth, it is characterized by the single mark of quiescence; seventh, it receives all the competing currents of rivers; eighth, its tides do not miss their appointed times; ninth, it can serve as a place of refuge for others; and tenth, it is never exhausted.
What is this great treasure trove?
It is like the great ocean, from which all manner of jewels emerge, yet they are not diminished when people take them.
The Bodhisattva is likewise; though boundless sentient beings practice with faith, the treasure trove of their merit is never diminished.
Just as the great ocean is deep, vast, and difficult to cross, so too is the Bodhisattva; no celestial Māras or non-Buddhists can cross the great ocean of their *prajñāpāramitā*.
Just as the ocean is boundless, so too is the Bodhisattva; their merit and wisdom are vast and limitless.
Just as the ocean gradually deepens, so it is with the bodhisattva, who becomes progressively deeper through the attainment of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).

For example, just as the great ocean does not harbor corpses, so too the Dharma-ocean of the bodhisattva does not cohabit with the corpses of all fetters, outflows, afflictions (*kleśa*), or evil associates (*pāpamitra*).

Just as all the streams that flow into the great ocean become of one single taste, so it is with the bodhisattva: all their merits, upon reaching the ocean of omniscience, likewise become of one single taste.

Just as the great ocean can accommodate all flowing streams without increasing or decreasing, so too it is with the bodhisattva: they receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas and explain them to the multitude, yet there is neither increase nor decrease.

Just as the tide of the great ocean does not miss its time, so too is the Bodhisattva; regarding the sentient beings they have brought to maturity, they likewise do not overstep the limits of their timing.
Just as the great ocean serves as a dwelling place and refuge for all large-bodied beings, so too does the Bodhisattva serve as a dwelling place and refuge for all sentient beings of great mind.
"Just as the great ocean is inexhaustible, so too is the Bodhisattva; for all sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma according to their needs without end.
According to the meaning of this passage, it refers to the Buddha.
How is this known to be so?
It is because it is said that the single flavor of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) does not allow for the lodging of fetters, outflows, or the corpse [of ignorance].
Furthermore, because Bodhisattvas retain their afflictions until those afflictions are exhausted, they have not yet perfected the knowledge of all modes.
Regarding the term "Bodhisattva," it is named according to the cause, or it may encompass both cause and effect.
Because these ten meanings exist, he is praised as being like the ocean.
In this present sutra, we shall for now rely on the third single meaning—being like the ocean—while the others will be omitted for brevity.

If one follows the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, it says: "For example, just as the great ocean remains unmoved by whatever comes to oppose it, so too is the arousal of the mind associated with the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*)."
Just as the great earth, so too is the initial generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*), for it can produce and sustain all the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*).
Just as the king of mountains, so too is the generation of the mind associated with the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), for nothing can shake it, being free from distraction.
There are parables for the six perfections, the four means of integration, the four immeasurables, and so forth; this briefly illustrates the third and fourth.

"Like space" refers to the third exhaustion, that of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), among the inexhaustible phrases in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, because it serves as a reflection for the remainder.
Sūtra: "By all my accumulated roots of goodness, may I swiftly attain the state of the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Commentary: The following twenty-five verses constitute the section on making aspirational prayers.
This is divided into two parts:
first, five verses on the aspiration for the benefit of oneself and others; second, twenty verses on the aspiration for the benefit of others alone.
Within the first part, there are further two sections:
The first three verses seek the aspiration for the fruit, while the final two verses seek the aspiration for the cause.
Within the initial aspiration for the fruit, there are two parts;
this half-verse seeks the aspiration for self-benefit regarding the fruit.

Sūtra: “Extensively expounding the True Dharma to benefit all sentient beings, causing them all to be liberated from manifold sufferings, and subduing the hosts of the powerful Māra armies, you shall turn the unsurpassed wheel of the True Dharma.”

Abiding for inconceivable numbers of kalpas, you satisfy sentient beings with the flavor of nectar; just like all the Victors of the past, you have perfected the six pāramitās, extinguished all greed, hatred, and delusion, subdued the afflictions, and eliminated all suffering.
The commentary states:
These two and a half verses express the aspiration for the benefit of others through the attainment of the fruit.

Within them: the first half-verse aspires that they may attain analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); the next half-verse aspires that they may subdue the celestial Māras; the next half-verse aspires that they may attain *nirvāṇa*; the next half-verse aspires that they may cultivate the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); and the final half-verse aspires that they may eliminate the six hindrances.
As understood from the words of the scripture:

"May I always attain the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), being able to remember hundreds of thousands of past births; may I also constantly recollect the Honored Muni, and may I hear the profound Dharma of all Buddhas."

By means of these various roots of goodness, may I serve the boundless and most supreme Honored One; may I remain far removed from all unwholesome causes and constantly practice the truly wondrous Dharma.
The commentary states:
The following two verses express the aspiration for the cause.
Briefly, there are four aspirations:
The first half-verse expresses the aspiration for the knowledge of past lives;

the second half-verse expresses the aspiration for the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). Regarding the six recollections—recollection of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, ethical discipline, generosity, and the devas—only two are mentioned here by way of illustration.
The final half-verse expresses the aspiration for virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
The following half-verse expresses the aspiration to abandon evil and cultivate goodness:
“May all sentient beings in every world be entirely freed from suffering and attain peace and happiness; may those whose sense faculties are incomplete have their physical forms made fully complete.”
The commentary states:
The following twenty verses clarify that [the bodhisattva’s conduct] consists solely of benefiting others.
This section has two parts:
The first sixteen verses pray for others to attain worldly fruits; the subsequent four verses pray for others to attain supramundane fruits.
Within the former [section], there are two parts:
the first fourteen verses pray for the attainment of present fruits, and the final two verses cause the attainment of future fruits.
The present section on the results has two parts:
first, seven verses wishing for the removal of suffering; second, seven verses wishing for the attainment of happiness.
Within the first part, there are three sections:
This first verse generally indicates the extraction from suffering.

The Sūtra says: "If there are sentient beings who encounter the suffering of illness, their bodies emaciated and having no support, may all their ailments be eliminated, and their faculties, physical appearance, and strength be fully restored."
The Commentary states:
Next, the following five and a half verses specifically clarify the departure from suffering.
There are five [points]:
This is the first verse, which extracts [beings] from the suffering of various diseases.

The Sūtra says: "If one violates the laws of the king and deserves execution, oppressed by manifold sufferings and giving rise to distress, when such extreme suffering is endured, there is no refuge capable of providing protection."
Commentary: The following three verses concern the second [section], the extraction of the suffering of punishments.
This has two parts:
The first verse indicates that there is suffering and no rescue.

The Sūtra says: "If one undergoes flogging, caning, shackles, and fetters, with various instruments of torture cutting into the body; when immeasurable hundreds of thousands of anxieties and afflictions arise, they oppress the body and mind, leaving not even a moment’s peace."
May all be granted freedom from bondage, as well as from the suffering of whips and staves; may those facing execution be granted their full lives, and may all their sufferings be forever eradicated.
The commentary states:
The following two verses are intended as vows for the eradication [of suffering].

Within these, the first one and a half verses cause one to be free from the sufferings of shackles, fetters, whips, and staves; the subsequent half-verse causes one to be free from the sufferings of mutilation and the severance of life.

Sūtra: “If there are sentient beings oppressed by hunger and thirst, may they obtain various kinds of sublime flavors; may the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame be able to walk, and the mute be able to speak.”

The commentary states: Within this there are two [purposes]: the third is to cause them to be free from the suffering of hunger and thirst; the fourth is to cause them to be free from the suffering of incomplete sense faculties.

The Sūtra says: "May impoverished sentient beings obtain a treasury of jewels, with storehouses overflowing so that they lack for nothing; may they all attain supreme and wondrous bliss, such that not a single sentient being suffers affliction."
The commentary states:
The first half-verse of the latter section causes one to leave behind the suffering of poverty; the second half-verse of the latter section concludes by causing one to leave behind all suffering.

Sūtra: "All humans and devas delight in beholding them; their deportment is gentle and refined, and they are exceedingly majestic. All experience immeasurable happiness in the present, enjoying abundant prosperity and being endowed with merit."
The commentary states:
The following seven verses express the aspiration for others to attain happiness.
There are twelve [verses] in total; herein, there are two [sections]:
The first half-verse causes one to obtain the respect, affection, and joy of humans and devas; the second half-verse causes one to obtain an abundance of various precious playthings and delights.

As the Sūtra says: "In accordance with the sentient beings' thoughts of music and song, wondrous sounds manifest before them all. When they think of water, a cool pond immediately appears, with golden lotuses floating upon its surface."
The commentary states:

There are two kinds of happiness here; the first half-verse brings about the happiness of obtaining music according to one’s thoughts, while the second half-verse brings about the happiness of obtaining ponds according to one’s wishes.

Sūtra: “In accordance with whatever those sentient beings think of in their minds—food, drink, clothing, and bedding; gold, silver, precious jewels, and exquisite lapis lazuli; necklaces and all manner of ornaments—they shall be fully provided.”
The commentary states:

There are two kinds of happiness here; the first half-verse causes one to obtain the happiness of mindfulness of the four requisites, while the second half-verse causes one to obtain the happiness of ornaments such as necklaces and strings of the seven precious gems.

Sūtra: “May sentient beings not hear evil sounds, nor may they see anything discordant; may their physical appearances all be dignified and majestic, and may each, with a heart of loving-kindness, cherish one another.”
The commentary states:

There are two kinds of happiness herein. The first half-verse brings about the happiness of a beautiful reputation and harmonious concord; the second half-verse brings about the happiness of physical excellence and compassionate affection.

Sūtra: “All worldly requisites for livelihood and various means of pleasure are fully satisfied whenever they are brought to mind; whatever precious wealth one obtains, one bestows it upon all sentient beings without any stinginess.”
The commentary states:

There are two types of happiness here; the first half-verse brings about the happiness of obtaining requisites according to one's wishes, while the second half-verse brings about the happiness of non-attachment and the happiness of giving.

Sūtra: "Incense for burning, powdered incense, and unguents, along with various exquisite flowers of manifold colors, fall from the trees three times each day; as they are enjoyed according to one's wish, joy arises."

May all sentient beings universally make offerings to the most supreme Honored Ones of the ten directions, to the pure and wondrous Dharma-gates of the Three Vehicles, and to the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
The commentary states:

"There are two types of joy herein; the first verse brings about the joy of obtaining incense and flowers at will, while the subsequent verse brings about the joy of making offerings to the Triple Gem."

Sūtra: “May I always vow never to dwell in a lowly or base station, nor to fall among the eight difficulties of the leisureless; may I be born as a noble among those who possess leisure, and may I forever have the fortune to attend upon the Buddhas of the ten directions. May I always be born into wealthy and honorable families, where treasures and granaries are all full; may my countenance and reputation be peerless, and may my lifespan extend for many kalpas.”
The commentary states:
The final two verses express the aspiration that others may attain future fruits.
There are five [points]:

The first half-verse causes one to attain the joy of being free from birth in the eight difficult states; the next half-verse causes one to attain the joy of constantly encountering the World-Honored One; the next half-verse causes one to attain the joy of always being born into wealth and nobility; the next single line causes one to attain the joy of an exquisite form and renown; and the final single line causes one to attain the joy of an extended lifespan.

Sutra: "May all women be transformed into men, valiant, courageous, intelligent, and possessed of great wisdom; may they always practice the bodhisattva path and diligently cultivate the six perfections to reach the other shore."
The commentary states:
The following four verses cause others to attain supramundane fruits.
